paras: The threatened lynching of William Bohan took place at Rockaway Beach, Long Island, New York, on August 3, 1888, when an angry crowd gathered at the police lockup where Bohan, a saloon keeper accused of gouging out his wife's eyes, was held. The crowd dispersed after a constable told it that the prisoner had already been taken away, and Bohan was moved to the Queens County Jail for his safety. The threat was reported only by the New-York Tribune; most papers dwelt instead on the assault, which the Evening World called 'one of the most horrible and fiendish acts ever recorded', and on Bohan's sentence of about twenty-seven years.

Bohan kept a saloon at Rockaway Beach and was the second husband of Kate Bohan, of Fairview avenue. According to later reports, he had torn out one of her eyes in April 1886 or 1887, but she pleaded for him, and he said at his trial that Justice Healy had discharged him. The Evening World blamed that outcome on his saloon and a political 'pull'.
In late July 1888 he was accused of gouging out her remaining eye with his thumb, leaving her blind.

After his arrest on Friday, Bohen was locked in the cells at police headquarters, and word of it spread along the Beach. Within a short time an angry crowd gathered, and people 'loud in denunciation of his crimes' openly threatened to lynch him. Constable Jones persuaded the crowd that the prisoner was not in the building but had been taken to the jail at Long Island City, and the Tribune wrote that Bohen was 'trembling in his cell until the mob dispersed'. No attack on the lockup and no injuries were reported.

According to the Tribune, Bohen was arraigned the next day before Edmund J. Healy of Far Rockaway and remanded to the Queens County Jail, a step it called necessary to save him from the people of the Beach. By August 10 his wife was said to be near death, and Coroner Cronin took her ante-mortem statement. That day Bohan was arraigned before Justice Edwin J. Healy, held without bail for the grand jury and sent back to the county jail, 'as it was not thought safe to keep him in the lockup at Rockaway Beach', while the Tribune added that open threats of lynching had been made. No report of arrests among the crowd appears in the coverage.

A grand jury returned two indictments, one for each assault. At his trial in the Queens County Court of Sessions at Long Island City on September 17, his wife testified that her first injury had been an accident, while her daughters and her sister described his threats and beatings. He was found guilty of mayhem, pleaded guilty to the second indictment the next day and received sentences of twelve years six months and fourteen years seven months at hard labor in Sing Sing.

The Tribune headed its report 'A Narrow Escape from Lynching', presenting the crowd's fury as a response to Bohen's crimes and the constable's ruse as what saved him, without criticizing the crowd. Its follow-up of August 11 repeated that open threats of lynching had been made. No other paper in the coverage mentioned the crowd, and no report named the race of anyone involved.

Elsewhere the coverage centered on the assault: an Evening World editorial called Bohan a 'monster' and a 'wretch' and argued that the death penalty was as justly his due as if he had murdered his wife. A New York dispatch printing his wife's ante-mortem statement ran in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union.

The trial drew wider notice, with headlines such as 'Bohan's Doom' in the Evening World, 'An Eye for an Eye' in the Rock Island Daily Argus and 'She Loves Him Yet' in the Atlanta Constitution, which credited its account to the World. These reports dwelt on the blinded wife's loyalty to her husband and on his appearance, and short items on the verdict ran as far away as St. Paul.

Accounts differ on the dates of both assaults (July 20, 30 or 31 for the second) and on which eye was lost first: the wife's ante-mortem statement named the right eye, while trial reports named the left. The Tribune also gave two arraignments before a Justice Healy, on August 4 and August 10, with different first names for the justice.

bases: An angry crowd gathered at the lockup where Bohan was held and openly threatened to lynch him, dispersing only when a constable told them he had been moved (A1, A5).
Bohan was not harmed: the crowd that threatened to lynch him over the assault on his wife dispersed after a constable's ruse, and he was later tried and sentenced in court (A1, A5, A6).
The crowd and the lynching threats appear only in two New-York Tribune items (A1, A5); the many other reports of the assault and trial do not mention them (A3, A6, A9, A12).

accounts.gist: Her husband had plucked out her right eye two years earlier and on July 20 gouged out the other, she thought with his thumb.

accounts.label: Mrs. Bohan at trial
accounts.gist: She testified that the first injury was an accident in the dark and that he never threatened her.

accounts.label: Trial reports
accounts.gist: Daughters and a sister testified to his threats and beatings; he was found guilty of mayhem, pleaded guilty to the second assault and was sentenced to about twenty-seven years.

framing.detail: The Tribune's 'A Narrow Escape from Lynching' described the crowd's fury as a response to his 'crimes' without criticizing it, and described the constable's ruse as saving him.
The Evening World editorial called Bohan a 'monster' and 'wretch' and said the death penalty was as justly his due as if he had murdered his wife, without mentioning the crowd.
Trial reports carried headlines such as 'Bohan's Doom', 'An Eye for an Eye' and 'She Loves Him Yet', centered on the wife's loyalty and the sentence.
